event: Super Typhoon Haiyan (Yolanda) storm surge, Tacloban / Eastern Visayas
deaths: About 6,300 (NDRRMC figure widely reported); a storm surge of more than 5 m hit Tacloban
languages: English technical term 'storm surge' used in warnings to Waray- and Tagalog/Filipino-speaking coastal communities
language_issue: The English technical term 'storm surge' meant nothing to many residents. Survivors called it a tsunami. Search-result summaries of Rappler (quoting a PAGASA official) and Devex say PAGASA admitted 'the storm surge wasn't explained in the warnings distributed to the public', and that the problem was 'how the information was translated, explained and disseminated'. Malacañang then had to ask the public not to use 'storm surge' and 'tsunami' as if they meant the same thing.
quantified_evidence: No survey figure was found. Evidence is qualitative: officials admitted the term was not understood, and a ScienceDirect paper found that 'local residents did not understand the meaning of the term storm surge'.
policy_change_after: PAGASA now pairs the English term with the Filipino 'daluyong ng bagyo' and gives surge heights in metres (PAGASA storm-surge information page; Manila Bulletin 2025 explainer).

event: October 2017 Sonoma Complex / North Bay wildfires (Tubbs etc.); also 2017 Thomas Fire and 2018 Camp Fire
deaths: About 44 across the North Bay fires (commonly reported figure)
languages: English-only evacuation warnings; large Spanish-speaking (and Indigenous Mexican-language, e.g. Mixteco) farmworker population
language_issue: California State Auditor: 'During those wildfires, none of the counties issued warnings directing people to evacuate in languages other than English... some people likely did not receive potentially life-saving emergency information in a language that they could understand.' Community radio KBBF and bilingual volunteers filled the gap with Spanish information.
quantified_evidence: Grist (2021): in the affected California counties '1 in 3 residents' speak a language other than English at home. Nationally, about 67 million people speak a language other than English at home.
policy_change_after: California SB 160 (chaptered 2 Oct 2019) requires every county to build cultural competence, including emergency communications, into its emergency plan. Sonoma County produced a 'culturally responsive' Emergency Operations Plan (2022) and an Office of Equity. Ventura and Santa Barbara hired full-time Spanish-speaking public information officers.

event: 31 May 2013 El Reno tornado and Oklahoma City flash flooding
deaths: 'over 20 people' (KGOU), including a Guatemalan family who sheltered in a drainage ditch / storm drain
languages: English warnings vs Spanish-speaking Latino (Guatemalan) residents
language_issue: A National Weather Service assessment found a 'lack of warning and forecasting resources in Spanish and residents weren't prepared'. The Guatemalan family took shelter in a storm drain and drowned, the wrong action for a flash flood. NWS's Rick Smith warned that machine translation loses 'nuances and the different layers of meaning' that 'can literally make the difference between life and death'.
quantified_evidence: The search-summarised NPR/KGOU reporting counts seven victims of the 31 May tornado who sheltered in a storm drain, among them a Guatemalan family.
policy_change_after: Spanish-language severe-weather broadcasts on Spanish radio, a Spanish-speaking certified broadcast meteorologist, a Red Cross Spanish tornado app and a Spanish preparedness pamphlet (KGOU 2015). NWS later began Spanish-language products.

event: FCC multilingual Wireless Emergency Alerts rule (policy response)
deaths: n/a (policy)
languages: English plus 13 languages (Arabic, Chinese, French, German, Haitian Creole, Hindi, Italian, Korean, Portuguese, Russian, Spanish, Tagalog, Vietnamese) and American Sign Language
language_issue: The rule answers repeated English-only alert failures. Phones will hold pre-installed templates for 18 alert types (e.g. flash flood warning, hurricane, storm surge, tsunami, fire) and 'display the relevant template in the device's default language'.
quantified_evidence: 13 languages plus ASL and 18 hazard templates. Carriers must comply by 12 June 2028.
policy_change_after: This is the policy change. The template approach avoids errors from translating in real time during an emergency.

event: Cyclone Idai, Beira and central Mozambique
deaths: More than 600 in Mozambique (official figures widely reported); the three-country toll exceeded 1,000
languages: Portuguese (official, used for humanitarian and warning communication) vs Sena, Ndau, Chwabo, Lomwe, Xitshwa, Nyanja, Makhuwa. In Malawi: Chewa, Lomwe, Yao. In Zimbabwe: Ndau, Shona.
language_issue: Warnings and humanitarian information went out mainly in Portuguese. CLEAR Global / TWB: 'Only half the population can speak Portuguese, the official language. Portuguese comprehension rates are particularly low in rural areas and among women.' In Beira relocation sites, local languages 'are much better understood than even Portuguese'.
quantified_evidence: TWB found '41% of people do not understand written Portuguese'. TWB survey, April 2019: 33% of people surveyed in Beira lacked the information they needed in a language they understand.
policy_change_after: TWB/CLEAR Global produced crisis language maps and translated materials into Sena and Chwabo. A 2025 Journal of Southern African Studies article ('The Language Question in Disaster Prevention and Preparedness: The Case of Multilingual Mozambique') argues for local-language early warning.

event: Cyclone Preparedness Programme (CPP), a standing system tested in cyclones 1997, Sidr 2007, Amphan 2020 and others
deaths: The 1970 Bhola cyclone killed about 300,000 and the 1991 cyclone over 138,000. The 1997 cyclone killed 193 after about 1 million people were sheltered.
languages: Bangla, delivered face to face by local volunteers, plus language-independent flag signals
language_issue: Success. Warnings from the Bangladesh Meteorological Department are turned into local spoken Bangla by volunteers from the same villages, using megaphones and a three-flag visual code that needs no literacy. A set of 'three red-and-black flags (one flag means a cyclone could be forming, two means it's on its way and three means impact is imminent)'.
quantified_evidence: About 76,000 volunteers in 3,801 village units, who can spread BMD information 'in less than 15 minutes' (Geographical). In 1997, 'one million people to take refuge in shelters before the cyclone hit, which reduced the number of casualties to 193'.
policy_change_after: CPP was created in 1973 after Bhola. It has since expanded, including a push for more women volunteers, with UNDP support.

event: Typhoon Hagupit (Ruby), the first big test after Haiyan
deaths: Far fewer than Haiyan (exact official toll not verified here)
languages: Filipino and local languages; plain-language explanation of 'storm surge'
language_issue: After Haiyan, agencies rewrote warnings in plain local terms. Save the Children reported that in Haiyan 'Many children said they didn't understand the terms used... They didn't know what storm surge meant', so it began 'explaining terms more clearly'. Tacloban's mayor said the city was better prepared after Haiyan's lessons.
quantified_evidence: CNN (5 Dec 2014): 'More than half a million people in the typhoon's projected path sought refuge in evacuation centers.'
policy_change_after: Warnings rephrased around expected impact (surge height, 'like a tsunami'). RA 10639, the Free Mobile Disaster Alerts Act (20 June 2014), requires telcos to send free alerts.

event: Great East Japan Earthquake and Tsunami (and the 1995 Hanshin precedent); 'Yasashii Nihongo' (Easy Japanese) and multilingual JMA warnings
deaths: About 18,000–19,000 dead or missing in 2011 (widely reported)
languages: Standard Japanese warnings vs foreign residents (Chinese, Korean, Portuguese, Tagalog, Vietnamese, Nepali, etc.). The response added Easy Japanese plus 14 foreign languages.
language_issue: Uekusa (2019): 'disaster warnings and announcements were only made in the de facto languages, English and Japanese respectively' (Christchurch and Tohoku). The Easy Japanese idea comes from 1995, when 'The proportion of foreign nationals killed and injured was higher than that for Japanese citizens, as calls to evacuate and safety warnings did not adequately reach them' (Nippon.com). Hirosaki University found disaster information 'more easily understood when conveyed in simple Japanese than in English or Chinese'.
quantified_evidence: Yasashii Nihongo for disasters is designed to be understood by about 80% of foreign residents (Nippon.com). JMA and the Fire and Disaster Management Agency built multilingual dictionaries of about 7,000 entries in 15 languages (including Japanese) covering Earthquake Early Warnings, tsunami warnings and evacuation instructions.
policy_change_after: Easy Japanese used by municipalities and NHK (NEWS WEB EASY). JMA website and warnings in 15 languages. The government's Safety tips app. Official Easy Japanese guidelines (2020).

event: Canterbury (2010) and Christchurch (22 Feb 2011) earthquakes
deaths: 185 (Feb 2011, widely reported)
languages: English-only official communications vs migrant / CALD communities (e.g. Chinese, Korean, Japanese, Filipino)
language_issue: Uekusa (2019): 'disaster warnings and announcements were only made in the de facto languages, English and Japanese respectively'. Linguistic minorities also struggled afterwards with recovery, insurance and mental-health services delivered only in English.
quantified_evidence: None found. Evidence is qualitative (interviews).
policy_change_after: Christchurch City Council commissioned 'Best Practice Guidelines for Engaging with CALD Communities in Times of Disaster' (Wylie, March 2012). The Christchurch Migrant Inter-Agency Group published lessons learned. Multilingual radio messaging and community-leader information hubs.

event: February–March 2022 NSW / Northern Rivers floods (Lismore and Sydney)
deaths: Four Lismore residents drowned (HRW). Three CALD (Tamil / Sri Lankan and Chinese background) people died in Sydney (SBS).
languages: English-only emergency alerts vs CALD communities (Tamil, Chinese, Arabic, Korean, Vietnamese, etc.)
language_issue: SBS (10 Mar 2022): NSW SES confirmed emergency alerts were not available in other languages. Only generic website information existed in simplified Chinese, Arabic, Korean, Vietnamese, Greek and Italian. SES spokesperson: 'The fact that we've had three deaths tragically from CALD communities... we will look at very seriously during the after-action review process.'
quantified_evidence: HRW: 'Emergency services knocked on only 2 of 15 interviewed households' doors'. Up to 3,000 rescue calls were lost. The NSW inquiry found the risk 'was not adequately communicated'.
policy_change_after: NSW SES public information campaign in six languages. The NSW Reconstruction Authority ran a flood-awareness campaign built for CALD audiences.

event: Tropical Cyclone Trevor, Ngukurr and Gulf communities (and later Indigenous-language practice for Cyclones Fina 2025 and Narelle 2026)
deaths: No deaths reported from Trevor in NT; the harm documented was panic and self-evacuation
languages: English BoM warnings vs Kriol, Yolŋu Matha, Anindilyakwa, Tiwi, Maung
language_issue: ABC (6 Apr 2019): 'Lack of Indigenous language translations intensified community panic'. Ian Gumbula: 'The explanation in English is very hard to understand. In the context of local languages like Kriol, certainly they could understand it.' NT Police had only pre-recorded Kriol preparedness messages, not rolling updates. The Chief Minister's department had no formal policy on translating emergency messages.
quantified_evidence: Hundreds of Ngukurr residents self-evacuated. In the very remote NT, 72.5% of the population is Indigenous and 86.8% speak an Indigenous language at home (BoM).
policy_change_after: BoM now works with Yolŋu Radio and the NT Aboriginal Interpreter Service. Advice is simplified into plain English, then translated. Interpreters in Tiwi, Yolŋu Matha and Maung worked during Cyclone Fina. For Cyclone Narelle (2026), recorded messages were issued in English, East Side Kriol, Anindilyakwa and Yolŋu Matha.

event: Yellowknife wildfire evacuation
deaths: None reported in the Yellowknife evacuation
languages: English and French alerts only, in a territory with nine official Indigenous languages (e.g. Wıìlıìdeh / Tłı̨chǫ Dene)
language_issue: The Conversation (Sara Wilson, SFU, 9 Dec 2025): 'emergency alerts were issued only in English and French'. Indigenous-language-first Elders had to rely on relatives, radio hosts or social media to interpret urgent instructions. Canada's NPAS 'currently supports message delivery only in English and French', although the CAP-CP standard can carry multiple language feeds and recorded audio.
quantified_evidence: Nearly 20,000 residents evacuated. Of 1,307 broadcast alerts issued in 2019–2022, none were in Indigenous languages.
policy_change_after: None yet. The author proposes pre-scripted templates, partnerships with community broadcasters, and AI translation under Indigenous oversight.

event: Remnants of Hurricane Ida flash flooding, basement apartment deaths
deaths: 11 NYC basement deaths, nearly all Asian (Chinese, Nepali, Korean) immigrants
languages: English (and Spanish) alerts vs Chinese, Nepali, Korean and other immigrant languages
language_issue: NWS issued NYC's first-ever flash flood emergency just before 9:30 pm on 1 Sept. Victims were mostly Asian immigrants in illegal basement units, 'a group for whom language access and risk messaging pose a significant challenge'. A search-result summary of The City Reporter (2024) says the city admitted to the federal government that communicating only in English and Spanish was a shortfall.
quantified_evidence: Per the same City Reporter summary, between 40% and 80% of households in the neighbourhoods where deaths occurred spoke other languages. Not independently verified: the page returned HTTP 429.
policy_change_after: Notify NYC 'Basement Alerts' launched 26 April 2023 in 14 languages (CBS New York). Few subscribers use non-English alerts.

event: January 2025 Los Angeles wildfires (Palisades, Eaton, Hurst, Hughes)
deaths: Not captured here
languages: Alerts in English and Spanish only vs Chinese, Korean, Tagalog, Vietnamese, Cantonese, Thai, Punjabi, Hindi
language_issue: UCLA study: according to LA County officials, emergency alerts were 'limited to English and Spanish due to system limitations'. Some Asian residents avoided evacuation centres because there were no interpreters.
quantified_evidence: More than 12,000 of about 50,000 Asian residents in the four fire zones need language assistance, 15% of the zones' total population (UCLA).
policy_change_after: Community groups (AAPI Equity Alliance) produced resources in six languages. The FCC 2028 template mandate is pending.

event: Maui (Lahaina) wildfire
deaths: About 100 (102 widely reported)
languages: English vs Ilocano, Tagalog, Chuukese, Marshallese, Pohnpeian, Tongan, Spanish
language_issue: The main warning failure was not about language (outdoor sirens were not sounded). But 36% of Lahaina residents spoke a language other than English at home, and interpretation was 'not adequately offered' for several Pacific and Filipino languages during response and recovery (Disaster Housing Recovery Coalition).
quantified_evidence: 'an estimated 36% of those who called Lāhainā home speaking a language other than English at home'. In a Hawaii DOH household survey, 87% named English as their primary language, 6% Ilocano.
policy_change_after: Governor's emergency memo on language access for the Maui wildfires (EM-23-07, 2023). The Hawaii Office of Language Access produced Ilocano and other resources.

event: Kerala floods
languages: Malayalam warnings vs interstate migrant workers (Hindi, Bengali, Odia, Assamese speakers)
language_issue: Peter, Sanghvi & Narendran (2020): migrants 'had missed the alerts in local languages resulting in poor preparedness'. Insight Turkey commentary (Irudaya Rajan et al.): the non-Malayalee population could not 'follow the warnings and instructions given by the authorities in Malayalam'. Fake news of dam collapses spread among migrants and sent crowds to railway stations.
quantified_evidence: None specific to language comprehension found.
policy_change_after: For COVID-19, Kerala 'circulated [messages] in Assamese, Odia, Bengali, Hindi and Tamil' and engaged officials who speak workers' languages. Kerala is building multilingual early warning for guest workers (South First).

event: Cyclone Phailin (2013) and Cyclone Fani (2019)
deaths: Phailin: 21 plus 23 in later flooding. Fani in Odisha: a few dozen (the 1999 super-cyclone killed more than 10,000).
languages: Odia (local language) plus English
language_issue: Success. Warnings were pushed through many local-language channels. For Fani, authorities used SMS, sirens, 43,000 volunteers and 'public address systems blaring messages in local language' (search-result summary of NYT / Business Standard / WEF coverage). The state SATARK system gives 'actionable advisories in both the local Odia and English languages'.
quantified_evidence: Phailin: about 1 million evacuated across 18,000 villages (World Bank). Fani: 1.2 million or more evacuated. '1.8 crore SMS messages were sent out by Location Based Alert System (LBAS) and Group Based Alert System (GBAS)'. About 1.5 million people moved to 9,177 shelters within 24 hours.
policy_change_after: Odisha's 'zero casualty' model with the OSDMA, community cyclone shelters and volunteer task forces. SATARK (Odisha) and national SACHET provide alerts in Odia.

event: 2022 monsoon super-floods (Sindh, South Punjab, Balochistan)
deaths: About 1,700 (widely reported NDMA figure)
languages: Urdu (official, used in messaging) vs Sindhi, Saraiki, Balochi, Punjabi, Pashto. Low literacy, especially among women.
language_issue: CLEAR Global / Pattan comprehension study (Feb 2023). A participant said: 'We can only understand voice messages. It is better if it is in Balochi or Saraiki. Urdu is difficult for us to understand.' UNESCO notes a 'forwarding paradigm' in which technical alerts pass between administrative levels 'without being translated into localized and actionable guidance'.
quantified_evidence: Per a search-result summary of the CLEAR Global study, '71% of the population does not have access to information', worse in Khairpur, Sanghar, Mirpur Khas and Dadu. Urdu ranks fourth as a first language. National literacy is 59% (68% men, 50% women).
policy_change_after: CLEAR Global recommends voice messages in regional languages. UNESCO is working on localising flood early warning.

event: August 2026 glacial/landslide-triggered flash floods, Nepal–China border corridor
deaths: Over 1,000 (CNN, 31 Aug 2026). Mongabay reports 1,252 dead and 4,216 missing. Figures were still changing.
languages: SMS alerts in Nepali only, on a corridor with a major trekking route (foreign tourists) and speakers of other languages
language_issue: Mongabay (Sept 2026): 'The alerts only went out in Nepali, on a corridor that includes a major tourist trekking route.' Researcher Chandani Bhandari: SMS warnings 'lacked exact locations, severity, context and actionable instructions'. Informal phone calls through trusted community networks worked better and often arrived first.
quantified_evidence: A head teacher moved about 900 students to high ground after community warning calls.
policy_change_after: Calls for cell broadcast, which can alert every phone in an area 'in multiple languages', and for binding SOPs linking forecasts to action (Bhandari & Dixit 2022).

event: NDMA drought early-warning bulletins issued in English; youth translate them into Turkana (Turkana County)
deaths: n/a (drought / food security)
languages: English bulletins vs Turkana (and other local languages). Many recipients cannot read.
language_issue: Government bulletins 'are distributed to county governments in English', so for many rural Kenyans 'they are of little help'. Hussein Noor Adille (Nawiri): 'People who cannot read will not understand the risks they will be facing.' Unpaid youth volunteers translate them for word of mouth and local radio. One translator: 'Sometimes the language used in the bulletins is difficult to understand.'
quantified_evidence: None. Benefits reported are qualitative (herders managing livestock better, parents preventing child malnutrition).
policy_change_after: None formal. Volunteers ask government to recognise and pay translators: 'We would do more if the government recognised this is a valuable service and compensated us.' NDMA community weather monitors use local-language radio.

event: Cyclone Freddy, after the post-Idai early-warning reforms
deaths: Fewer than 200 (WMO), against more than 600 for Idai
languages: Local languages via community radio (e.g. Changana in Gaza) and a 3-2-1 toll-free line (Portuguese, Changana, Macua)
language_issue: Success after reform. UNDRR (search-result summary): 'Radio announcers convey early warning messages in local languages in each district'. One announcer at Chokwe-Kendlemuka community radio (Gaza) activated local committees. Callers can dial 3-2-1 free to hear messages in Portuguese, Changana or Macua. WMO: warnings 'were disseminated through community radio stations and trained volunteers.'
quantified_evidence: About 500 people took early action after the Chokwe community radio announcements (UNDRR). WMO reports damages fell from US$3 billion (Idai) to US$500 million (Freddy) and deaths from more than 600 to fewer than 200.
policy_change_after: This is the post-Idai/Kenneth reform: INGC (now INGD) local risk-management committees, community radio, 3-2-1 local-language line.

event: Storm Daniel, Derna dam collapses
deaths: 'At least 4,352' dead and about 8,000 missing (HRW)
languages: Arabic (shared language, so the failure was contradictory content, not translation)
language_issue: Counter-example: everyone shared the language, but the messages contradicted each other. At 1:12 am the Water Resources Ministry said 'all dams in Derna had been inspected and were in good condition'. At 2:59 am it said the dams 'had reached their capacity', but they had already collapsed at 2:40–2:50 am. A curfew imposed on 10 Sept overrode the mayor's 9 Sept evacuation order for five neighbourhoods.
quantified_evidence: Forecasters issued warnings 72 hours ahead. HRW: 'There's good reason to believe that the storm would have been far less deadly had the authorities responded to the danger signs by evacuating people.'
policy_change_after: Calls for an independent investigation (HRW, Amnesty). No consolidated reform documented.

event: DANA flash floods, Valencia province
deaths: At least 232 (224 in Valencia province) per judicial count cited by Wikipedia. The Wikipedia infobox gives 240–248 overall.
languages: Bilingual ES-Alert (Spanish and Valencian)
language_issue: The ES-Alert began to be drafted at 18:15 but was sent at 20:11, after most victims had died. In the court investigation (Dec 2025), emergency sub-director Jorge Suárez testified that consellera Salomé Pradas and Vicent Mompó 'obligaron a cambiar "cosas por tema lingüístico" en la versión valenciana', such as removing the accent from 'València' and replacing 'tipus' and 'aquest' with 'tipo' and 'este'. He named this as one of several causes of delay. Pradas disputes his account; the judge refused a face-to-face confrontation (El Español, May 2026).
quantified_evidence: About 1 h 56 min from starting the draft (18:15) to sending (20:11). Civil Protection had requested the alert at 18:35.
policy_change_after: Ongoing judicial investigation. The case argues for pre-approved bilingual templates so that editing text cannot hold up a warning.

event: Ahr Valley / Rhineland-Palatinate and North Rhine-Westphalia floods
deaths: About 135 in the Ahr valley, more than 180 in Germany (widely reported)
languages: German (shared language, so the failure was in what the warning meant and what it told people to do)
language_issue: Counter-example: the language was shared, but the wording did not convey the danger or say what to do. At 19:35 KATWARN warned of water above 5 m, well over the 100-year level of about 3.7 m. It still advised people to avoid cellars, stay off flooded roads and clear drains. Houses were half under water by 20:30.
quantified_evidence: Thieken et al. (2023): '35 % of the respondents from NW and 29 % from RP did not receive any warning'. Of those warned, '85 % did not expect very severe flooding and 46 % reported a lack of situational knowledge on protective behaviour.'
policy_change_after: Germany introduced cell broadcast (DE-Alert/Cell Broadcast) in 2023 and reformed its warning mix.

deaths: About 1,800 (widely reported)
languages: English-only broadcasts vs Vietnamese and Spanish speakers
language_issue: Grist (2021): 'many Vietnamese and Latino immigrants had a harder time understanding storm warnings and evacuation orders, since the broadcasts were only in English'.
